store.2: My favorite class this semester is definitely Advanced Algorithms. I'm a huge fan of theory when it connects directly to real-world problem-solving. I find it fascinating to explore how we can optimize pathfinding in large networks or find the fastest way to handle huge datasets with minimal time complexity. The class dives into dynamic programming approaches and approximation algorithms for NP-hard problems, which can be mind-bending at times. However, our professor is great at explaining these concepts in an intuitive manner. She'll present a seemingly impossible problem and then show us a strategy to approximate a solution. Every time I leave that class, my brain is buzzing with ideas and insights.

store.4: I'm also taking a Distributed Systems course(CS 2631), which is probably the second hardest. It's a lot of reading, group discussions, and we're working on a major project that simulates a decentralized file storage system. The group project is an adventure in itself. We have to collaborate with folks who have different coding styles and sometimes different ideas of what the final product should look like. However, that's also the beauty of it. In a real-world setting, you're never working in a vacuum. You have to be able to integrate your code with others' and handle everything from concurrency issues to node failures gracefully. It's nerve-wracking at times, like when I spent hours troubleshooting a weird bug that turned out to be a single misplaced bracket in one of the config files. But once we got that fixed and everything ran smoothly, it was a huge sense of accomplishment.

store.6: I'm also taking an elective in Game Design, which counts toward my major if I combine it with certain other classes. As a gamer at heart, this was a must-take. The professor is actually from the industry; he worked on a couple of indie games that got some decent traction. We're learning about basic 2D and 3D engines, implementing physics, and even a bit of user experience design. It's unbelievably fun because every assignment is super creative. Getting that design right was tricky, but it was also rewarding to see it come together.

store.8: I also have an Introduction to Quantum Computing class, which sounds super cutting-edge, I know. Initially, it was intimidating, but the professor's approach is to focus on conceptual understanding rather than pure math. Of course, there is math involved, like linear algebra, but it's interspersed with code examples in frameworks that simulate quantum circuits. We're not actually building quantum computers or anything, but we're modeling basic algorithms like Grover's and Shor's to see how they theoretically outperform classical methods. It's mind-blowing stuff and has made me rethink how I approach problems.

store.10: I'm also taking a Capstone Project course, which is basically the sink-or-swim part of senior year. We have the entire semester to conceptualize, design, and build a software solution that solves a real problem. My group and I decided to work on a project that uses machine learning to analyze social media sentiment for better emergency response. It's a fancy-sounding project, but essentially, we're building an interface that city officials or campus security could use to see real-time alerts by analyzing a firehose of tweets or posts for words that might suggest a disaster or crisis. This project is pulling together everything I've learned as a CS major: database management, building an API, front-end interface, and the ML pipeline. We're also learning about project management and how to keep ourselves organized. One person on our team is the designated "Scrum Master," so each week we have sprints, daily stand-ups, and all that agile jazz. It's a lot, but if we can pull it off, I'll be super proud.

store.12: I'm also taking a Philosophy of Mind class, which is my last required non-CS elective. I chose it because it ties back into AI in interesting ways. We discuss consciousness, the concept of mind, and how it might apply to artificial intelligence. It's a smaller class, so we do a lot of class discussions, which is a nice change of pace from all the coding in my other classes. Sometimes it's nice to just sit back and analyze abstract ideas. This class also helps me see the bigger picture, like the ethical implications of building AI systems that could one day mimic or simulate human thinking. Two weeks ago, I wrote a paper on whether strong AI could ever truly experience qualia, like the subjective experience of color or pain. It's a huge topic in the philosophy world, and it was such a trip to research. I think bridging technical knowledge with ethical considerations is important, so I'm grateful for that perspective.

I start with Advanced Algorithms at 9:30 am, followed by a short break before heading to my Distributed Systems lecture at 11:00. After lunch, I have the Capstone meeting, which can be a mix of lectures, lab work, and project team time. Tuesdays and Thursdays are a bit lighter with Quantum Computing in the morning and Game Design in the afternoon. Philosophy of Mind is on Thursday evenings, which can be tough if I'm tired from the rest of the day. Fridays are open, but I usually end up working on assignments, group projects, or labs. I also do some undergrad research hours in a lab focused on data visualization for big scientific data sets. It's interesting, but it definitely adds to the workload.

store.20: I've been involved in undergraduate research since the end of my sophomore year, and it's been a fantastic experience. It's given me a glimpse into how knowledge is created in the tech world, and I'm proud to be a part of it. As a freshman, I didn't initially see myself going down the research route. I was more focused on coding projects and hackathons. However, one of my professors noticed my ability to bridge technical coding with user experience and suggested I apply for a research assistant position in a lab focused on data visualization for big scientific datasets. I was initially hesitant due to the intimidation factor, but I decided to take the leap, and it turned out to be a great decision.

store.41: I'm a fourth-year Computer Science student, and I've seen how the culture has evolved over the years. I've discovered different communities that make this place feel like a second home. There are many ways to get involved beyond just coding in front of your laptop all day.
store.42: I joined the Computer Science Society, which hosts weekly meetups where we discuss new technologies, share personal projects, and have industry speakers. It's a welcoming environment for beginners. I can chat with fellow members who might have worked on similar topics in an internship if I'm stuck on a tricky concept.
store.43: I've been attending the VR/AR Club on and off since my sophomore year. I got hooked once I started doing research in immersive analytics, so it was natural for me to want to hang out with people who share that passion. The club is hands-on—they have a VR lab in the engineering building with headsets, sensors, and quirky prototypes built by past members. We host demos where each person shows off their latest project, whether it's a mini-game or something more experimental like AR interfaces for everyday tasks. I just love the supportive vibe when people are excited about emerging tech.
store.44: I occasionally pop into the student-run radio station events, like their open-mic nights. It's a blast to see people sing, read poetry, or perform stand-up comedy. I remember one night, a friend from my Distributed Systems class performed an acoustic set. He's usually so quiet in class, but on stage, he was belting out these soulful tunes as if he was born for it. Moments like that remind me there's always more to someone than meets the eye when you're just coding together or doing group projects.
store.45: The campus has these iconic spots, like the central lawn where students hang out between classes. Student organizations set up booths there, and you can see fliers for everything from an a cappella group to an environmental activism society. They hand out freebies like stickers or candy to lure you into signing up for their mailing list. My personal kryptonite is free pizza, so whenever a club includes that in their advertisement, they can easily tempt me. The lawn is also where some of the biggest campus events take place, like our annual Tech Fest. During Tech Fest, different project teams put up posters, do live demos of their prototypes, and recruiters sometimes roam around looking for potentially innovative ideas. It's a big deal here, especially for engineering and CS folks.
store.46: I think campus culture is fairly collaborative. There are pockets of competition, especially among seniors trying to land top internships or job offers, but overall, people want to help each other succeed. I remember the campus hackathon in my second year, which was a huge eye-opener. Thousands of students from various backgrounds crammed into the student center for 24 or 36 hours straight, hacking away. It was chaotic but exhilarating. You'd see beginners learning the basics of GitHub while advanced teams used complex machine learning libraries to do real-time image recognition. Sponsors and mentors wandered around to see if anyone needed help. I formed a small team with a few casual acquaintances, none of us were super close friends. But the bond we formed during that all-nighter, eating stale pizza at 3 a.m., debugging code, and deliriously cheering each other on, was unlike anything I'd experienced before. That's the vibe I associate with campus life: you're all in the trenches together, forging friendships through these shared experiences and challenges.
store.47: Dorm life can be a huge part of campus culture. In my first two years, I stayed in a dorm specifically for engineering majors, which we jokingly called "The Engi-House." Late-night coding sessions in the common lounge were legendary. Someone would be banging away on an assignment for Data Structures, while another group might be streaming e-sports tournaments. Occasionally, that environment got a little too intense, with stressed-out engineers fueled by energy drinks. However, it also meant that if you ran into a stumbling block, there was always someone nearby who could offer a quick pointer. Beyond academics, we'd hold potlucks, watch Netflix together, or even host a small talent show to blow off steam.
store.48: I've been volunteering at outreach events, particularly the "Tech for Good" day organized by our CS department. Local high school students come to campus to learn about programming and problem-solving. I help run mini-workshops on topics like web development or basic Python. It's rewarding to see younger students light up when they manage to make a simple game or animated webpage. I remember how I felt at that age, feeling overwhelmed by the tech world. Giving them a positive first experience is something I take pride in. Events like that show a different side of campus: it's not just about academic research or class assignments; it's about engaging with the community and inspiring the next generation to get excited about STEM fields.
store.49: We have a lively social scene beyond academics. Greek life is an option for those interested, but I didn't join a fraternity. Instead, I found that specialized clubs are a great way to meet people with shared interests. For example, a friend who's into robotics joined the Robotics Team in his first semester and found a second family there. They now hang out on weekends, watch movies together, and grab dinner. I've also grown close to folks in the VR/AR Club and the CS Society. We don't just talk shop when we're together; we joke around, complain about cafeteria food, or plan weekend trips to the local hiking trails.
